passage: After news of a riot in a city far away, Farhana stopped waiting at the bus stop. Farhana, who shared her Eid sewaiyan with Rashmi every year, now answered messages with one word. In their small town near Nashik, Rashmi, fifteen, felt a cold knot in her stomach. Jatin from class whispered that Farhana's family had warned her to stay away. Rashmi did not want to believe it. On Saturday she carried a packet of pakoras to Farhana's house. Farhana's mother let her in, and Farhana stared at the floor. "Have I done something?" Rashmi asked. "No," Farhana said finally. "Ammi is scared people will blame us for what strangers did." Rashmi shook her head. "I don't blame you for anything you didn't do. You're my friend." They ate the pakoras on the roof. On Monday Farhana was at the bus stop.

qa.q: What did Rashmi bring to Farhana's house?
qa.a: Rashmi brought a packet of pakoras.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when Farhana stopped answering properly?
qa.a: Rashmi felt worried and hurt, with a cold knot in her stomach, but she did not want to believe the rumour.

qa.q: Which choice by Rashmi kept the friendship alive?
qa.a: Rashmi went to Farhana's house, asked honestly whether she had done something, and said she did not blame Farhana for what strangers did.
Farhana's mother was scared that people would blame their family for what strangers did, so Farhana stayed away out of fear and shame.

grounding: A teenager finds a friend of another faith pulling away after a news event and keeps trust alive by staying in touch and asking honestly.

passage: Kwame, fifteen, noticed that Ines had started eating lunch in the library. She used to save him a seat in the canteen and swap almond biscuits for his mum's plantain chips. Now she only nodded. Ines's family went to the mosque on Fridays, and Kwame sang in his church choir, and until now it had never mattered. After a week, Kwame texted, "Did I do something?" Ines wrote back, "No. My grandmother says I should stay with my own community after what was said about us on the news." The next day he found her at the tram stop. "I saw the news too," he said. "I don't think you or your family did anything. I'd hate to be blamed for what a stranger did." Ines's shoulders dropped. "I didn't want to bring trouble." "You're not trouble. I miss the biscuits." She laughed, the first time in a week.

qa.q: Where did Kwame find Ines the next day?
qa.a: Kwame found Ines at the tram stop.

qa.q: How might Kwame have felt when Ines began eating lunch in the library?
qa.a: Kwame probably felt puzzled, worried and a bit hurt, which is why he texted to ask whether he had done something.

qa.q: Which choice by Kwame kept the friendship alive?
qa.a: Kwame asked honestly by text, then went to find Ines and said he did not blame her or her family for what a stranger did.
Ines's grandmother told her to stay with her own community after what was said on the news, and Ines did not want to bring trouble to Kwame.

grounding: A teenager finds a friend of another faith pulling away after a family warning and keeps trust alive by asking honestly and refusing to blame the friend.
